root.note: Wiktionary: from Gothic *raupa, from raupjan ‘to pluck’. The Gothic noun is reconstructed, not attested.

history: Roupa, ‘clothes’, began as loot. The Visigoths and Suebi who ruled Iberia after Rome spoke Germanic languages, and their word for what was plucked or taken, Gothic *raupa, entered the local Latin. Clothes were probably among the most valuable things a soldier could take, and the word slid from ‘plunder’ to ‘garments’. Portuguese still has a verb from the same family, roubar, ‘to steal’. A roupa is a collective noun: a roupa means ‘the clothes’, the laundry, everything on the washing line. A single item is uma peça de roupa. You put a roupa in the máquina de lavar roupa. English robe and French robe, ‘dress’, are cousins.
historyEinfach: Roupa means ‘clothes’. The word comes from the Goths, a Germanic people. In their language, it meant things you take from enemies. The Portuguese verb roubar, ‘to steal’, is from the same family. English robe is related.

elsewhere.text: French made the same jump from loot to clothes, and then to a dress.
Spanish ropa is the same word, with the older single vowel.
